summary:
During the hackathon, we developed the "SubStellar|SPHEREx" website, a resource for the rapid analysis of how celestial objects change over time. The site includes a search function that lets users find the object they need by name or coordinates. We implemented a timeline that allows a frame-by-frame review of an object's changes over a chosen period, and users can select the number of frames themselves.

The SPHEREx telescope collects a huge amount of data about the universe, and it is easy to get lost in it, even for scientists, let alone ordinary people. Our website turns these complex terabytes of numbers into a clear visual format. Thanks to it, searching for changes across hundreds of images becomes as simple as watching a time-lapse video.
details:
On the application's homepage, users initiate a search by entering a space object's name or coordinates, selecting the desired detector spectral bands (D1–D6), and setting a frame limit (30, 60, 100, or 180). While the loading screen is displayed, the system automatically retrieves all images of the specified sky area from NASA archives, filtering out outdated duplicates in favor of the latest data versions and caching results for instant subsequent requests. To reduce the load on primary archive servers and ensure reliability, the download process uses a hybrid architecture: if the main cutout server is unresponsive, the pipeline seamlessly switches to AWS S3 cloud storage to independently crop the required sky fragment.

When archives return hundreds of images, a specialized algorithm selects frames evenly, up to the chosen limit, across all observation periods and spectral bands, ordering them chronologically. Each frame undergoes an automated cleaning process to remove cosmic dust background glow, mask dead matrix pixels, and eliminate isolated cosmic ray strikes. Because the telescope captures objects on different dates and at different rotation angles, the system aligns all frames to a unified orientation (North facing up), enhances faint details, and saves them as lightweight web-ready images.

In the final processing stage, the cleaned frames are combined by time epochs into composite color images. Longer infrared spectral bands are mapped to red, medium to green, and shorter to blue; if only two bands are selected, the system automatically synthesizes the intermediate green channel. The gentle background cleaning applied earlier preserves intricate structures like galactic spiral arms and gas-dust nebulae. By comparing individual epochs against an averaged deep-sky image, users can easily identify moving objects like asteroids, which typically disappear during the averaging process.

Once processing is complete, the final images and metadata are delivered to the browser for smooth timeline navigation on the results page. This main dashboard features a right-hand sidebar summarizing the user's input data, while the central interface is divided into three key blocks: dynamic date and spectral band information, an interactive photo gallery navigable via buttons and a sun-shaped control, and a brief educational overview of the telescope itself.
